examples.problem:
Suppose we wish to find a zero of the function $\boldsymbol{f}(x,y)$ in the region $[-2,2] \times [0,2] \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,$ where
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14074434/assets/0f5dda7937b1ffed646730040efe11464d46ef1f3ec6ae5dacf84075bd5be01b.png)
Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process that starts with $\mathbf x_0 = \big[1, \: 2 \big]^T.$
examples.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $\boldsymbol{f} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is

$$
\mathbf{x}_{n+1} = \mathbf{x}_n - [J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)]^{-1} \boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n),
$$

where $J_\boldsymbol{f}(\mathbf{x}_n)$ is the Jacobian of $\boldsymbol f$ evaluated at $\mathbf{x}_n.$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y-x-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y-x-2) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}-y+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}-y+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2xy-1 & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14074434/assets/c3ec90119193ca9c0cb886bc7b7c698eb155e6a801fd267c0a17a0d329eff84d.png)

Starting with ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14074434/assets/eff9e5b8ab46002bd82fa42d59f60b1bb78ca04228d7c73b52d131d222ccb894.png) we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{[\begin{aligned}2xy-1 & {x}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & 2xy-1\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}y-x-2 \\ x{y}^{2}-y+1\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}2(1)(2)-1 & (1)^{2} \\ (2)^{2} & 2(1)(2)-1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}(1)^{2}(2)-1-2 \\ 1(2)^{2}-2+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{3\cdot 3-4\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 13\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{11}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2.2 \\ -0.6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
